title: Kingston v. Preston
summary: An apprentice had to provide the agreed security for payment before he could compel the transfer of his employer’s business.

sections.Parties: Kingston was an apprentice who expected to acquire a share of a silk-mercer’s business. Preston was the mercer who was to retire and transfer the business.
sections.Material Facts:
The arrangement contemplated that, after a year and a quarter, Preston would retire and the business would be carried on by Kingston and a partner chosen as provided in the agreement. Kingston was to pay for his share in monthly installments of £250. To protect those payments, he promised good and sufficient security approved by Preston, to be supplied at and before execution and delivery of the transfer deeds.

Preston did not transfer the business. Kingston sued, and Preston pleaded that Kingston had failed to provide the security. The argument for Preston emphasized that Kingston lacked sufficient resources to make an unsecured promise a satisfactory substitute.
sections.Procedural History: Kingston demurred to Preston’s defense, maintaining that the security promise was independent and that Preston had to transfer the business and then sue separately. The King’s Bench entered judgment for Preston.
sections.Issue: Were the promises independent, or was provision of security a condition that had to occur before Preston’s duty to transfer the business became due?
sections.Holding: The security undertaking was a condition precedent to Preston’s transfer obligation. Its nonperformance defeated Kingston’s action.
sections.Reasoning:
Mansfield distinguished independent promises, dependent promises requiring prior performance, and concurrent promises requiring readiness and an offer to perform. The classification depended on the evident purpose and sequence of the transaction rather than the order of clauses in the document.

Security was central to the contemplated installment sale. Requiring Preston to surrender a valuable business first would deprive him of the protection for which he contracted and leave him dependent on Kingston’s unsecured personal promise. The intended order therefore made the security necessary before the transfer.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Kingston supplies the basis for understanding why one party may withhold its performance when the return performance on which it depends has not occurred.

topics.conditions: The promised security was required before transfer of the business.
topics.constructive-conditions: The relationship and intended order of performances determine their dependence.
topics.interpretation: The court infers dependence from the transaction’s purpose.
topics.risk-allocation: Security protects a party who would otherwise perform first without assurance of receiving payment.
